desc:
You may pick any subset of nums (the empty subset is allowed, its sum is 0). Let S be the sum of the picked elements. Return the minimum possible value of |S - goal|.

nums = [7, -9, 15, -2], goal = -5
best subset: {-9, 7, -2} with sum -4
result = 1

Elements can be negative, so the usual knapsack table over sums does not apply.
hints: There are 2<sup>30</sup> subsets, which is too many to enumerate, and the sums are too large for a DP table. Split the array in two halves.
Each half has at most 2<sup>15</sup> subsets. Any subset of the whole array is a subset of the left half plus a subset of the right half. List the sums of both halves.
Sort both lists of sums. For each left sum x, you need the right sum closest to goal - x. As x increases, that target decreases, so a pointer on the right list only moves down: two pointers.
editorial: This is the meet-in-the-middle technique. Split nums into a left half and a right half of at most 15 elements each and list all subset sums of each half (at most 32,768 values per list). A subset of the whole array corresponds to exactly one pair (left sum, right sum), and the total is their sum.

Sort both lists, L ascending and R ascending. For each x in L in increasing order, we want the value y in R closest to goal - x. Keep a pointer j at the largest index with x + R[j] ≤ goal; as x grows, j can only move left, so the pointer travels at most |R| steps in total. The best partner is either R[j] (just below or on the goal) or R[j+1] (just above it); evaluate both and keep the smallest distance.

Time is O(2n/2 · n) for generating and sorting the lists, plus O(2n/2) for the sweep, instead of O(2n). Memory is O(2n/2). Initialise the answer with |goal|, the empty subset, which also covers an empty array.
